statement: A convex polygon has interior angles that are all different whole numbers of degrees. What is the largest number of sides it can have?

choices.misconception: I took the exterior angles of a polygon to add up to 180° and fitted $1 + 2 + \dots + 18 = 171$ under that total.
I solved $n(n + 1)/2 = 360$, got about 26.3 and rounded up to 27, but 27 different exterior angles need at least 378°.
I counted how many different whole numbers an interior angle can be, 1° to 179°, and ignored the angle sum.
I let every exterior angle be 1°, forgetting that the interior angles, and so the exterior angles, must all be different.

hints: Look at the exterior angles instead of the interior ones.

The exterior angles of a convex polygon add up to 360°. If the interior angles are different whole numbers, so are the exterior angles. Make the exterior angles as small as possible to fit in as many as you can.
The smallest possible exterior angles are 1°, 2°, 3° and so on. Find the largest $n$ with $1 + 2 + \dots + n \le 360$.

solutions.reliable: Each exterior angle is 180° minus an interior angle, so the exterior angles are different positive whole numbers of degrees, and they add up to 360°. With $n$ sides they total at least $1 + 2 + \dots + n = n(n + 1)/2$. Since $26 \times 27 / 2 = 351 \le 360$ but $27 \times 28 / 2 = 378 > 360$, there are at most 26 sides. And 26 is possible: take exterior angles 1°, 2°, ..., 25° and 35°, which are different and add up to $325 + 35 = 360$, giving interior angles 179°, 178°, ..., 155° and 145°. A convex polygon with any such exterior angles exists, because the side lengths can be chosen to close the shape. The transferable idea: an extremal question about angles often becomes easy after switching to exterior angles, whose sum is fixed.

whyOnTest: Switching from interior to exterior angles turns a polygon question into fitting different whole numbers under a fixed total of 360.
